records.title: 15.4. Insonni tamg‘alamaslik: “shubhali” — “firibgar” degani emas
records.statement: Loyiha muallifi sifatida men fuqaroni shunchaki tizimda shubhali signal paydo bo‘lgani uchun “firibgar” deb atashni to‘g‘ri deb hisoblamayman. Firibgarlikning o‘zi yomon va zararli harakat bo‘lishi mumkin, lekin texnik indikatorning mavjudligi insonning aybdorligini avtomatik ravishda isbotlamaydi. Menimcha, insonning qilgan harakatini baholash bilan insonning o‘ziga tamg‘a qo‘yish o‘rtasida farq bor. Ayrim holatlarda odam noto‘g‘ri yo‘lga kirib qolishi, aldanishi, noto‘g‘ri muhit yoki ta’sirga tushishi, tajribasizligi yoki boshqa hayotiy sharoitlar sabab xato qilishi mumkin. Bunday sabablarni tushunishga harakat qilish o‘sha harakatni oqlash degani emas. Aksincha, sababni tushunish kelajakdagi holatlarning oldini olish uchun foydali bo‘lishi mumkin. Shu sababli FINZANJIRda asosiy yondashuv: indikator → risk → Cross-Match → Case → tekshiruv → vakolatli natija. Ya’ni tizim signal beradi, tekshiruvga yordam beradi, lekin signalning o‘zi insonni “firibgar” deb belgilamaydi

records.title: 15.5. Fuqaro va uning oilasi uchun ehtimoliy ahamiyat
records.statement: Moliyaviy zarar faqat hisobdagi raqamning kamayishi bilan tugamasligi mumkin. Inson katta zarar ko‘rsa, uning kundalik hayoti, rejasi va oilaviy sharoitiga ham ta’sir qilishi mumkin. Og‘ir moliyaviy vaziyat ayrim hollarda insonni yanada noto‘g‘ri qarorlar qabul qilishga undashi yoki boshqa salbiy oqibatlar xavfini oshirishi mumkin. Mening qarashimcha, xavfni oldindan kamaytirish yoki sodir bo‘lgan zararni imkon qadar tezroq cheklash orqali bunday og‘ir vaziyatlarning ayrimlarini oldini olishga hissa qo‘shish mumkin. Bu bilan inson va uning oila a’zolari uchun ham xotirjamroq sharoit yaratilishi ehtimoli bor. Bu yerda ham men kafolat bermayman. Loyiha barcha oilaviy yoki ijtimoiy muammolarni hal qilmaydi. Lekin moliyaviy xavfsizlikni yaxshilash insonning og‘ir vaziyatga tushib qolish ehtimolini kamaytirishga yordam berishi mumkin, degan qarashdaman

records.title: 15.6. Bankka bo‘lgan ishonch va fuqaroga qulaylik
records.statement: Men kelajakdagi kuchli tizimni faqat ko‘proq tekshiruv qiladigan tizim sifatida tasavvur qilmayman. Xavfsizlik bilan birga qulaylik ham muhim. Fuqaro o‘z pulidan foydalanayotganda doimiy qo‘rquvda bo‘lib qolmasligi, muammo yuz berganda esa qayerga va qanday murojaat qilishini tushunishi kerak. Agar xavfsizlik mexanizmlari to‘g‘ri tashkil qilinsa, fuqarolarning bank va to‘lov tizimlariga bo‘lgan ishonchi oshishi mumkin, deb o‘ylayman. Banklar esa o‘zining asosiy faoliyatiga ko‘proq e’tibor berib, xavfsizlik bilan bog‘liq takroriy va ortiqcha qo‘l mehnatini tizimli mexanizmlar bilan kamaytirish imkoniga ega bo‘lishi mumkin. Shu bilan birga, xavfsizlikni kuchaytirish fuqaroga keraksiz to‘siqlar yaratmasligi kerak. Kelajakdagi yechimlar xavfsizlik, qonuniylik va qulaylik o‘rtasidagi muvozanatni izlashga qaratilishi kerak

records.title: 15.7. Yangi xavflar paydo bo‘lsa, tizim ham rivojlanishi kerak
records.statement: Men FINZANJIRni bir marta ishlab chiqilib, keyin o‘zgarmaydigan tizim sifatida ko‘rmayman. Buning uchun yangi sxemalarni kuzatish, ularni qonuniy va ishonchli manbalar orqali o‘rganish, indikatorlarni tekshirish, False Positive va False Negative holatlarini tahlil qilish, model va qoidalarni sinovdan o‘tkazish hamda zarur bo‘lsa qayta kalibrlash kerak bo‘ladi. Agar tizimdan biror xavf o‘tib ketsa, buni faqat muvaffaqiyatsizlik sifatida ko‘rmasdan, undan qanday saboq olish mumkinligini ham ko‘rish kerak. Menimcha, kuchli himoya tizimi xatoni yashirmaydigan, undan bilim chiqarib, keyingi versiyani yaxshilaydigan tizim bo‘lishi kerak

records.title: 15.8. Xalqaro tajriba va kelajakdagi hamkorlik
records.statement: Kelajakda boshqa davlatlarda, jumladan Yevropadagi moliyaviy va kiberxavfsizlik tizimlarida qo‘llanilayotgan yondashuvlarni o‘rganish va ulardan foydali tajribalarni mahalliy sharoitga moslashtirish imkoniyatlarini ko‘rib chiqish kerak, deb hisoblayman. Bu “tayyor tizimni ko‘chirib olish” degani emas. Har bir davlatning qonunchiligi, bank tizimi, ma’lumotlarni himoya qilish talablari, texnik infratuzilmasi va fuqarolarning ehtiyojlari farq qiladi. Shuning uchun xalqaro tajriba o‘rganiladi, taqqoslanadi va faqat mos keladigan yondashuvlar kelajakdagi alohida loyihalar yoki rivojlanish bosqichlari uchun asos sifatida ko‘rib chiqiladi. Bunday hamkorlik hozirgi FINZANJIRning amaldagi imkoniyati sifatida emas, kelajakda o‘rganilishi mumkin bo‘lgan yo‘nalish sifatida qaraladi

records.title: 15.9. FINZANJIR — yakuniy nuqta emas, poydevor
records.statement: Men FINZANJIRni o‘z-o‘zidan yakuniy loyiha deb emas, keyingi bilim va ishlanmalar uchun poydevorlardan biri deb ko‘raman. Ushbu loyiha ustida ishlash davomida men ham yangi tajriba orttirishim, qaysi yo‘nalishlarda bilimimni chuqurlashtirishim kerakligini yaxshiroq tushunishim mumkin. Hozirda mening barcha tegishli yo‘nalishlar bo‘yicha tajribam yetarli darajada deb da’vo qilish noto‘g‘ri bo‘ladi. Aksincha, men ushbu loyihani ishlab chiqish jarayonining o‘zini ham o‘rganish jarayoni deb bilaman. Kelajakda kiberxavfsizlik, moliyaviy xavfsizlik, antifraud, xalqaro tajriba va boshqa tegishli yo‘nalishlarni chuqurroq o‘rganish, shu bilimlardan foydalanib alohida yangi loyihalar yaratish istagi bor. Bu yangi loyihalar FINZANJIRga shunchaki qo‘shib yuborilmaydi. Avval ular alohida o‘rganiladi, texnik va huquqiy jihatdan asoslanadi, keyin amaliy qiymati bo‘lsa alohida yo‘nalish sifatida rivojlantirilishi mumkin. Shu bilan birga, kelajakdagi o‘rganishlar FINZANJIRning o‘zini ham yanada kuchaytirish imkoniyatlarini ko‘rsatishi mumkin

records.title: 15.10. Moliyaviy resurs — maqsad emas, rivojlanish vositasi
records.statement: FINZANJIRni rivojlantirish istagimning asosiy sababi pul topish emas. Biroq katta loyihani ishlab chiqish, xavfsizlikni ta’minlash, mutaxassislar bilan ishlash, infratuzilmani yaratish va uzoq muddat davom ettirish uchun moliyaviy resurs zarur ekanini ham inkor qilmayman. Shuning uchun moliyaviy barqarorlikni maqsadning o‘zi emas, loyihani sifatli davom ettirish vositasi sifatida ko‘raman. Agar loyiha o‘zini rivojlantirish uchun yetarli resursga ega bo‘lsa, undan yangi bilim olish, yangi mutaxassislarni jalb qilish, xavfsizlikni kuchaytirish va kelajakdagi ishlanmalarni yaratish imkoniyati ham kengayadi. Mening asosiy istagim esa shu tajribalar orqali fuqarolarga hech bo‘lmaganda kelajakda yaxshiroq himoya va xavfsizroq muhit yaratish imkoniyati borligini ko‘rsatishdir

records.title: 15.11. Muallifning o‘z rivojlanishi va mas’uliyati
records.statement: Men ushbu loyiha bilan birga o‘zim ham rivojlanishim kerakligini tushunaman. Loyiha yaratishning o‘zi barcha javoblarni bilish degani emas. Aksincha, ayrim savollarni aniqlash, bilmagan narsalarni o‘rganish va mavjud qarashlarni yangi dalillar asosida qayta ko‘rib chiqish jarayonning bir qismidir. Shu sababli kelajakdagi yangi loyihalar ham bugungi FINZANJIR tajribasidan foydalanishi mumkin. Muvaffaqiyatli yechimlar ham, ishlamagan yondashuvlar ham tajriba beradi. Men bu tajribani faqat bitta loyiha doirasida yopib qo‘ymasdan, undan keyingi ishlanmalar uchun foydalanish kerak deb hisoblayman. Agar FINZANJIR kelajakda amaliyotga joriy etilsa, uning rivojlanishi ham to‘xtab qolmasligi kerak. Yangi xavflar, yangi texnologiyalar, yangi qonuniy talablar va yangi tajribalar paydo bo‘lishi bilan tizimni qayta ko‘rib chiqish imkoniyati saqlanib qolishi kerak

records.title: 15.12. Muallifning yakuniy qarashi
records.statement: Mening qarashimcha, FINZANJIRning asosiy ma’nosi faqat biror dastur yoki texnik platforma yaratishda emas. Uning ma’nosi rivojlanayotgan moliyaviy va kiber muhitda xavfsizlikni ham rivojlantirishga urinishda. Men fuqarolar pulidan doimiy qo‘rqib yashamasligini, muammo yuz berganda qayerga murojaat qilishini bilishini, banklar esa o‘z vazifalarini ishonchliroq bajarishi uchun xavfsizlik jarayonlari imkon qadar tizimli bo‘lishini istayman. Men barcha muammolar yo‘qolishini va’da qilmayman. Ammo bugungidan yaxshiroq himoya qilish, zararni kamaytirish, hodisalardan o‘rganish va kelajakdagi xavflarga tayyorlanish mumkin, deb hisoblayman. Shuningdek, insonni bitta texnik signal asosida yomon yoki “firibgar” deb tamg‘alashdan ko‘ra, holatni tekshirish, sababni tushunish va vakolatli tartibda xulosa qilish to‘g‘riroq, deb o‘ylayman. Xatoni tushunish uni oqlash emas; aksincha, kelajakda shu xatoning qayta sodir bo‘lish ehtimolini kamaytirish uchun bilim olishdir

records.title: 15.12. Muallifning yakuniy qarashi
records.statement: Shu nuqtai nazardan FINZANJIR men uchun yakuniy manzil emas. U tajriba, bilim va kelajakdagi yangi loyihalar uchun poydevor bo‘lishi mumkin. Men ham bu yo‘lda o‘rganishda davom etaman va imkoniyat bo‘lsa, boshqa yo‘nalishlarda ham foydali ishlanmalar yaratishni istayman

records.title: 15.13. O‘quvchiga qoldiriladigan yakuniy savol
records.statement: Agar texnologiya rivojlanar ekan, undan foydalanish bilan birga yangi xavflar ham rivojlanishi tabiiy bo‘lsa, biz kelajak uchun qanday moliyaviy va kiberxavfsizlik tizimlarini bugundan boshlab yaratishimiz kerak? Bu savolga ushbu hujjat tayyor javob bermaydi. U faqat FINZANJIR orqali bir yo‘nalishdagi qarashni ko‘rsatadi. Qolgan imkoniyatlar, yechimlar va kelajakdagi yo‘nalishlar esa yangi tajriba, tadqiqot va amaliy sinovlar orqali aniqlanishi mumkin

records.statement: FINZANJIRning maqsadi xavf signallarini imkon qadar erta aniqlash, kontekstlash, tushuntirish, audit izini saqlash va qonuniy recovery jarayonini qo‘llab-quvvatlash

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Master Flow konseptual ravishda ma’lumot/signallar → Validation → Normalization → Risk Engine → Cross-Match → Fraud Graph → Risk Signal/Explainability → Case Management → Human/Bank Review → Protection/Recovery → vakolatli natija → Audit/KPI → Feedback

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Master Flow kelajakdagi to‘liq platforma modelidir; hozirgi APKda real bank API, real-time Data Exchange, Production monitoring va to‘liq avtomatik orchestration mavjud deb da’vo qilinmaydi

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Risk Engine ruxsat etilgan signallarni kontekst va bog‘liqlik bilan tahlil qilib, qo‘shimcha tekshiruv zarurati haqida risk kontekstini shakllantirishga xizmat qiladi

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Risk Score signal mavjudligi, ishonchliligi va umumiy risk darajasini ifodalovchi analitik mexanizm; ballning o‘zi yakuniy qaror yoki firibgarlik isboti emas

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph hodisalar, qurilma, tarmoq, tranzaksiya, karta, hisob yoki qabul qiluvchi kabi qonuniy mavjud obyektlar orasidagi bog‘liqliklarni ko‘rishni osonlashtiradi; shaxsni avtomatik aybdor qilmaydi

records.statement: Case Management signal va kontekstni tekshiruvga yaroqli hodisa sifatida boshqarish, izlarni saqlash va vakolatli ko‘rib chiqishga tayyorlashga xizmat qiladi

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: Human/Bank Review avtomatik signalni vakolatli ko‘rib chiqishdan ajratadi; risk signali yakuniy huquqiy hukm emas

records.title: finzanjir_specific_card
records.statement: FIN-RECOVERY hodisadan keyin zararni kamaytirish, qonuniy nizolash/murojaat, izlarni saqlash va recovery imkoniyatlarini muvofiqlashtirish yo‘nalishidir

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Atoms consist of a nucleus and electrons described by quantum-mechanical states; chemistry connects structure to observable properties. Effect: Bonding and reactivity depend on electron structure. Example: Compare carbon isotopes with the same atomic number but different neutron counts. Counterexample: An isotope is not a different element when proton number is unchanged. Common misconception: Atomic number is proton count, not total nucleon count. Calculation: For an isotope, mass number A = Z + N. Practical situation: Use periodic-table data and distinguish atomic number from mass number. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e covers atomic structure and periodic relationships

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chemical bonding describes interactions that lower or organize the energy of atoms and molecules. Effect: Bond type and geometry influence melting point, solubility, conductivity and reactivity. Example: NaCl behaves differently from molecular sugar because their bonding/structures differ. Counterexample: Covalent does not automatically mean nonpolar. Common misconception: Ionic compounds are not simply “molecules of ions”; their lattice structure matters. Calculation: Formal charge bookkeeping can test a Lewis structure. Practical situation: Explain bonding without treating simple labels as absolute categories. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e provides chemical bonding and structure frameworks

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Stoichiometry relates quantities of reactants and products through a balanced chemical equation. Effect: It enables prediction of required reactant or expected product amounts. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives a 2:1 mole ratio for H2:O2. Counterexample: A coefficient is not the same as a subscript. Common misconception: Moles are not grams; conversion requires molar mass. Calculation: n = m/M; use equation coefficients for mole ratios. Practical situation: Check units at every conversion step. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e quantitative chapters support mole and reaction calculations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates and factors that influence them. Effect: Changing rate does not necessarily change equilibrium composition. Example: A catalyst can lower activation energy for an alternative pathway. Counterexample: A catalyst does not create energy or guarantee a favorable reaction. Common misconception: Faster reaction does not mean more product at equilibrium. Calculation: Rate laws are determined experimentally for a reaction. Practical situation: Do not infer a rate law solely from the balanced equation unless justified. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry covers kinetics and mechanisms

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal. Effect: Changing conditions can shift composition until a new equilibrium is established. Example: Adding a reactant can shift a system toward products in appropriate cases. Counterexample: Equilibrium does not mean equal concentrations of reactants and products. Common misconception: Equilibrium is not a stopped reaction. Calculation: K expressions follow stoichiometric exponents in the balanced equation. Practical situation: State temperature and reaction when interpreting K. Evidence: OpenStax explicitly describes dynamic equilibrium and equilibrium calculations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Acid-base chemistry concerns proton transfer, electron-pair interactions and related equilibrium models. Effect: Buffers resist pH change over a useful range but have finite capacity. Example: A weak acid can have a strong effect when concentrated enough; strength and concentration differ. Counterexample: Weak acid does not mean harmless or always dilute. Common misconception: pH is logarithmic, not a linear concentration scale. Calculation: pH = -log10(a_H+) in the idealized aqueous treatment. Practical situation: Do not use pH alone to diagnose health conditions. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry provides acid-base and equilibrium foundations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Organic chemistry studies carbon-containing molecular structures, reactions and properties. Effect: Small structural changes can change physical and chemical properties. Example: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula but different connectivity and properties. Counterexample: Same molecular formula does not guarantee same compound. Common misconception: “Organic” does not mean natural or safe. Calculation: Molecular formulas can be checked against atom counts; structure requires connectivity information. Practical situation: Avoid safety claims based solely on the word organic. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry includes organic chemistry and functional-group foundations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chemical thermodynamics relates energy, heat, work, entropy and free energy to physical and chemical change. Effect: A negative ΔG indicates thermodynamic favorability in the stated convention, not reaction speed. Example: A process can be spontaneous yet slow. Counterexample: Spontaneous does not mean instantaneous. Common misconception: ΔG<0 is not a statement that a process is fast. Calculation: Under common constant-T,P conditions, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Practical situation: State conditions and distinguish thermodynamics from kinetics. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e covers entropy, laws of thermodynamics and free energy

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chemistry calculations connect symbolic equations to measurable quantities with dimensional analysis. Effect: Dimensional errors can reveal incorrect setup even when arithmetic is correct. Example: For molarity, c = n/V when n is moles and V is liters. Counterexample: A numerical answer without units is incomplete in physical chemistry. Common misconception: Molarity and molality are not interchangeable. Calculation: c1V1 = c2V2 applies to simple dilution assumptions. Practical situation: Track units and assumptions explicitly. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry quantitative chapters support these calculation frameworks

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Cells are basic organizational units of life with specialized structures performing coordinated functions. Effect: Membrane properties regulate exchange with the environment. Example: Mitochondria and chloroplasts illustrate specialized cellular roles. Counterexample: Not all cells have a nucleus; prokaryotic cells differ. Common misconception: “Cell = tiny bag” misses regulated internal organization. Calculation: Diffusion rate depends on gradients and physical conditions rather than a single universal number. Practical situation: Use microscopy/diagram context and distinguish prokaryotic and eukaryotic organization. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e provides cell structure and function foundations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Cell membranes regulate movement of substances through selective permeability and transport mechanisms. Effect: Transport affects cell volume, ion balance and signaling. Example: Water can move across membranes by osmosis. Counterexample: Osmosis is not simply “water always moves to salt”; membrane and solute conditions matter. Common misconception: Active transport is not synonymous with all protein-mediated transport. Calculation: Flux depends on gradients, permeability and transport properties. Practical situation: Describe the membrane and relevant solute before predicting direction. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers membrane structure and transport

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Genetics studies inheritance and variation through genes, genomes and their expression. Effect: Variants can alter traits, but phenotype can also depend on environment and regulation. Example: A genotype can contribute to a phenotype without uniquely determining it. Counterexample: A gene is not identical to a visible trait. Common misconception: “Dominant” does not mean better, more common or more powerful. Calculation: Punnett-square probabilities apply only under stated inheritance assumptions. Practical situation: Separate population frequency, dominance and phenotype. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e provides genetics and inheritance foundations

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations across generations. Effect: Population frequencies can change through selection, drift, mutation and gene flow. Example: Genetic drift can change allele frequencies even without adaptive advantage. Counterexample: Individuals do not evolve genetically because they “need” to. Common misconception: Evolution is not a ladder toward perfection. Calculation: Allele-frequency change can be calculated from population counts under defined models. Practical situation: Distinguish individual adaptation during life from population evolution across generations. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers evolution, natural selection and population genetics

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Ecology studies interactions among organisms and their physical environment across levels of organization. Effect: Changes to one component can propagate through food webs and nutrient cycles. Example: Removing a key predator can alter prey and vegetation patterns. Counterexample: A food chain is not the whole ecosystem. Common misconception: Energy flow and matter cycling are different concepts. Calculation: Population growth models depend on assumptions and parameters. Practical situation: Use system boundaries and distinguish energy transfer from nutrient recycling. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers ecology and ecosystem processes

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy and supports carbon fixation in photosynthetic organisms. Effect: Photosynthesis links energy flow with atmospheric carbon cycling. Example: Plants use light, water and CO2 to synthesize carbohydrates while releasing oxygen in oxygenic photosynthesis. Counterexample: Plants do not obtain all of their food directly from soil. Common misconception: Photosynthesis is not simply “plants breathe in CO2 and make oxygen”; it is a coupled biochemical system. Calculation: Simplified overall equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Practical situation: Use simplified equations as summaries, not full mechanisms. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers photosynthesis and cellular energy

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Cellular respiration is a set of pathways that transfer chemical energy from fuels into ATP and other useful intermediates. Effect: ATP availability supports many cellular processes. Example: Glucose can be metabolized through glycolysis; downstream pathways depend on conditions. Counterexample: Respiration is not identical to breathing. Common misconception: Anaerobic fermentation is not simply “no metabolism.” Calculation: ATP yield depends on organism, pathway and accounting assumptions. Practical situation: Avoid presenting one fixed ATP number as universal. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers cellular respiration and fermentation

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Biological measurements require operational definitions, controls, uncertainty awareness and appropriate sampling. Effect: Poor sampling or confounding can produce misleading conclusions. Example: A controlled experiment changes one target factor while monitoring outcomes. Counterexample: Correlation alone does not establish causation. Common misconception: A statistically significant result is not automatically biologically important. Calculation: Mean, variance and confidence intervals summarize data under assumptions. Practical situation: Record units, sample size and measurement method. Evidence: OpenStax Biology emphasizes experimental methods and scientific reasoning

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Health is influenced by biological, behavioral, environmental and social factors, while health systems organize prevention, treatment and care. Effect: System capacity and access affect population health. Example: Vaccination is a preventive intervention; diagnosis and treatment are different steps. Counterexample: A chatbot cannot replace a clinician or health system. Common misconception: “Healthy” cannot be inferred from one symptom or measurement alone. Calculation: Risk is often probabilistic rather than deterministic. Practical situation: For symptoms or treatment decisions, defer to qualified professionals and current clinical guidance. Evidence: WHO health topics frame health across diseases, interventions, systems and determinants. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Medicines are regulated products used to prevent, treat or lessen disease effects, with benefits and risks that depend on context. Effect: Quality and correct use influence safety and effectiveness. Example: WHO emphasizes safe, effective, quality-assured medicines and regulation. Counterexample: A medicine being available does not make it appropriate for every person. Common misconception: Natural does not mean automatically safe; prescription status does not mean “dangerous” by definition. Calculation: Dose calculations require drug-specific, patient-specific and clinical assumptions. Practical situation: Do not provide individualized prescribing or dosing; use official guidance and clinicians. Evidence: WHO medicines guidance emphasizes quality, safety, effectiveness and regulation. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Vaccination trains immune defenses to reduce the risk and severity of specified infections. Effect: High coverage can reduce transmission for some infections while individual protection varies. Example: WHO states immunization prevents millions of deaths annually and is a key primary-health intervention. Counterexample: No vaccine gives absolute protection against every outcome. Common misconception: Vaccines are not identical to antibiotics and do not work by treating bacterial infections after the fact. Calculation: Effectiveness is measured under defined populations and outcomes; do not convert population estimates into personal certainty. Practical situation: Use national immunization schedules and clinician advice. Evidence: WHO vaccines and immunization guidance. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms no longer respond adequately to medicines that once controlled them. Effect: AMR increases treatment difficulty and risks of severe outcomes. Example: WHO describes AMR as a major global health threat and emphasizes coordinated action. Counterexample: AMR is not the same as the body becoming “immune” to an antibiotic. Common misconception: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as uncomplicated influenza. Calculation: Population-level AMR metrics cannot determine which drug will work for an individual. Practical situation: Never recommend self-starting or stopping antimicrobials; consult a clinician. Evidence: WHO AMR topic and 2026 fact sheet. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Public health protects and improves population health through surveillance, prevention, policy and community interventions. Effect: Effective interventions can reduce exposure and disease burden at scale. Example: Vaccination programs and outbreak surveillance are public-health examples. Counterexample: Public health is not simply hospital medicine at a larger scale. Common misconception: A population statistic does not automatically predict an individual outcome. Calculation: Rates and risks require a defined population, period and denominator. Practical situation: Use current official health agencies for outbreaks and rapidly changing guidance. Evidence: WHO health-topic framework and immunization/AMR guidance. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Diagnosis is a clinical process that integrates history, examination, tests and differential reasoning to identify a condition. Effect: Context and testing can change the differential substantially. Example: Fever can occur in many conditions, so fever alone is not a diagnosis. Counterexample: An online answer cannot establish a diagnosis without clinical evaluation. Common misconception: “One symptom = one disease” is unsafe reasoning. Calculation: Diagnostic tests have sensitivity, specificity and predictive values that depend on context. Practical situation: FINZANJIR AI should explain educationally and recommend professional care when appropriate. Evidence: WHO health topics demonstrate the breadth of conditions and interventions requiring context. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Mental health concerns involve emotional, cognitive and behavioral well-being and may require professional assessment. Effect: Support, early help and appropriate care can improve outcomes. Example: WHO lists mental health among major health topics. Counterexample: A chatbot should not label a person with a psychiatric diagnosis from a conversation. Common misconception: A difficult day is not automatically a disorder. Calculation: Screening scores are not equivalent to diagnosis. Practical situation: Use supportive language and urgent local help when safety risk is present. Evidence: WHO health-topic framework supports a broad, non-diagnostic approach. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Medical evidence links claims to studies, guidelines, surveillance and clinical context with varying certainty. Effect: Strong evidence can still have limits in populations or outcomes. Example: A randomized trial and an observational association answer different questions. Counterexample: One headline study is not automatically the final word. Common misconception: “Published” does not mean “proven.” Calculation: Effect size, uncertainty intervals and study design matter. Practical situation: Prefer current authoritative guidelines and multiple high-quality sources for high-stakes claims. Evidence: WHO pages illustrate the need for current, regulated health information. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: The Solar System consists of the Sun and objects gravitationally bound to it, including eight planets, dwarf planets, moons and smaller bodies. Effect: Different regions favor different compositions and planetary types. Example: Inner planets are rocky; outer giant planets are gas/ice giants. Counterexample: Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet under the IAU definition. Common misconception: The Solar System is not the same thing as the Milky Way. Calculation: Orbital periods can be related to distance and central mass under Keplerian approximations. Practical situation: Use current NASA/IAU definitions for classification. Evidence: NASA Solar System facts and exploration pages

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Exoplanets are planets beyond our Solar System detected and characterized through astronomical measurements. Effect: Different methods have different biases and detection limits. Example: Transit observations can reveal periodic dips in a star’s brightness. Counterexample: A detected exoplanet is not automatically habitable. Common misconception: Earth-sized does not mean Earth-like. Calculation: Transit depth roughly relates to the squared planet-to-star radius ratio under simple assumptions. Practical situation: Separate confirmed detection from candidate status and habitability claims. Evidence: NASA exoplanet resources describe multiple detection methods and diverse planet types

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Stars are self-gravitating luminous objects whose structure and evolution depend strongly on mass and composition. Effect: Stars create and distribute many heavy elements over cosmic history. Example: NASA describes stars as fundamental building blocks of galaxies and discusses stellar populations. Counterexample: All stars do not have the same lifetime or final state. Common misconception: Brightness alone does not uniquely determine mass. Calculation: Luminosity, flux and distance are linked by inverse-square behavior in simple isotropic cases. Practical situation: Use observed quantities with uncertainty and distance assumptions. Evidence: NASA star/exoplanet science resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system containing stars, gas, dust, dark matter and other components. Effect: Galaxy properties change over cosmic time. Example: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy according to NASA. Counterexample: A galaxy is not a single star system like the Solar System. Common misconception: “All galaxies look like spirals” is false. Calculation: Angular size and physical size require distance information. Practical situation: Distinguish observational classification from speculative interpretation. Evidence: NASA Solar System/galaxy educational resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Orbital motion results from gravity and initial motion, producing trajectories that can be approximately Keplerian in suitable systems. Effect: Changing energy or angular momentum changes orbital properties. Example: Earth remains in orbit because its tangential motion and solar gravity combine into a trajectory. Counterexample: Orbit does not mean gravity is absent. Common misconception: Astronauts are not “outside gravity”; they are in free fall. Calculation: For a circular orbit, v=sqrt(GM/r) under a point-mass approximation. Practical situation: State the two-body/circular-orbit assumptions. Evidence: NASA basic space-flight and Solar System resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Cosmology studies the universe on the largest scales, including its expansion, composition and history. Effect: Models can be updated when new observations challenge parameters or assumptions. Example: Galaxy redshift can provide evidence related to cosmic expansion in appropriate contexts. Counterexample: Cosmology is not the same as astrology. Common misconception: A model is not identical to a direct photograph of the entire universe. Calculation: Distances and redshifts require cosmological model assumptions for interpretation. Practical situation: Separate established observations from model-dependent inference. Evidence: NASA educational resources provide large-scale cosmic context

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Astrobiology and the search for life examine environments, biosignatures and planetary conditions that could support life. Effect: A potentially habitable environment is not proof of life. Example: NASA states that Earth is currently the only place where life is known. Counterexample: An atmospheric molecule alone may have non-biological sources. Common misconception: “Habitable” means potentially suitable, not inhabited. Calculation: Probability claims require explicit assumptions and base rates. Practical situation: Present uncertain life claims as hypotheses until evidence supports them. Evidence: NASA search-for-life and exoplanet resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Astronomical knowledge is built from light, timing, spectra, motion and statistical inference because direct sampling is usually impossible. Effect: Uncertainty determines how strongly a conclusion can be stated. Example: Parallax can estimate nearby stellar distances. Counterexample: A colorful telescope image is not necessarily a direct-color photograph. Common misconception: A measured signal is not automatically a confirmed interpretation. Calculation: Parallax distance uses d proportional to 1/p under defined units. Practical situation: Report uncertainty and method with astronomical measurements. Evidence: NASA exoplanet and solar-system science pages illustrate observation methods

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Plate tectonics describes large lithospheric plates moving relative to one another. Effect: Long-term plate motion reshapes Earth’s surface. Example: Convergent boundaries can include subduction. Counterexample: Earthquakes occur only at plate boundaries is too absolute. Common misconception: Plate tectonics is not the same as continental drift alone. Calculation: Plate velocity can be estimated from distance/time measurements. Practical situation: Use boundary type and local geology when interpreting hazards. Evidence: USGS explains plate tectonics and its relation to earthquakes and volcanoes

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Earthquakes are sudden releases of stored elastic energy associated with fault rupture and ground motion. Effect: Ground shaking can damage structures and trigger secondary hazards. Example: USGS monitors earthquakes and assesses hazards. Counterexample: Magnitude and intensity are not identical concepts. Common misconception: An earthquake cannot be predicted exactly from a simple calendar pattern. Calculation: Magnitude scales are logarithmic; do not treat increments as linear energy changes. Practical situation: Follow local seismic safety guidance; do not claim exact prediction. Evidence: USGS earthquake hazard resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Volcanoes are openings or structures through which magma, gases and volcanic material reach the surface or near-surface environment. Effect: Eruptions can produce lava, ash, gases and secondary hazards. Example: Volcanic hazards vary by volcano and eruption type. Counterexample: All volcanoes do not erupt explosively. Common misconception: Volcanoes are not simply “mountains that spit fire.” Calculation: Hazard probability is location- and time-dependent. Practical situation: Use official observatory alerts for real hazards. Evidence: USGS earth-science and hazard-monitoring framework

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: The water cycle describes continuous movement of water among atmosphere, land, oceans, ice and living systems. Effect: Changes in precipitation, storage or use affect water availability. Example: Rainfall can feed rivers, soil moisture and groundwater depending on conditions. Counterexample: Water does not simply move from ocean to cloud to river in one fixed path. Common misconception: The water cycle is a closed global cycle with no local water-management issues is misleading. Calculation: Water balance can be expressed as inputs minus outputs plus storage change. Practical situation: Define watershed and time period before calculating balance. Evidence: USGS water resources and National Geographic water-map resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes longer-term patterns and variability. Effect: Climate trends do not determine every individual day. Example: A cold day does not by itself refute long-term warming. Counterexample: Weather and climate are not synonyms. Common misconception: One measurement is insufficient to establish a climate trend. Calculation: Trend estimation requires defined period, data quality and statistical treatment. Practical situation: Use long-term datasets for climate claims. Evidence: National Geographic climate mapping and Earth-science resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Geohazards are natural Earth processes that can harm people or infrastructure, including earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes and floods. Effect: Preparedness and resilient design can reduce impacts. Example: Building codes can reduce earthquake losses even though they cannot stop earthquakes. Counterexample: Hazard is not identical to risk. Common misconception: “Natural disaster” does not mean impacts are unavoidable. Calculation: Risk can be conceptualized as a function of hazard, exposure and vulnerability; exact models vary. Practical situation: Use local hazard maps and official alerts. Evidence: USGS hazard monitoring and Earth-science education

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Earth materials include minerals, rocks, soils and sediments formed through geological processes. Effect: Material properties influence landscapes, resources and hazards. Example: The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic processes. Counterexample: Rocks and minerals are not interchangeable terms. Common misconception: Soil is not simply crushed rock; it includes organic matter and biological processes. Calculation: Mineral identification can use observable properties such as hardness, streak and cleavage. Practical situation: Use multiple properties rather than color alone. Evidence: USGS Earth-science educational framework

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Earth science links atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere as interacting systems. Effect: Feedbacks can amplify or damp changes. Example: Water, climate, land and ecosystems interact in drought and flood processes. Counterexample: Earth systems are not independent boxes. Common misconception: A single-variable explanation often misses coupled feedbacks. Calculation: System models track stocks, flows and feedbacks under assumptions. Practical situation: Make system boundaries and timescales explicit. Evidence: USGS and National Geographic Earth-system mapping resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Maps represent spatial information using symbols, scale, projection and coordinate systems. Effect: A map can simplify reality while preserving selected relationships. Example: A thematic map can show population density by region. Counterexample: A map is not the territory itself. Common misconception: Bigger visual area does not always mean larger real-world area. Calculation: Scale converts map distance to ground distance under the stated scale. Practical situation: Check projection, date, source and legend before interpreting. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker emphasizes maps as tools for analysis and storytelling

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Latitude and longitude provide a global coordinate framework for locating places. Effect: Correct coordinate order and datum matter for practical GIS use. Example: A location can be specified with latitude and longitude. Counterexample: Latitude and longitude are not interchangeable. Common misconception: Degrees alone without reference direction can be ambiguous. Calculation: Distance from coordinates requires a geodesic or projection-aware method. Practical situation: Keep N/S/E/W or signed-coordinate conventions explicit. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker includes latitude and longitude resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Physical geography studies Earth’s physical landscapes, climate, water, soils and natural processes. Effect: Climate and geology help explain spatial patterns. Example: Mountain relief influences climate and drainage. Counterexample: Physical geography is not only memorizing place names. Common misconception: One climate variable cannot explain every landscape. Calculation: Spatial comparisons require consistent units and scales. Practical situation: Use maps and multiple layers to connect processes to patterns. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker resources span physical geography, climatology and Earth science

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Human geography studies spatial patterns of people, cultures, economies, migration and settlements. Effect: Patterns change over time and can differ by scale. Example: Urbanization can change land use, transport and service demand. Counterexample: Human geography is not just population counting. Common misconception: A correlation between place and outcome does not prove a single cause. Calculation: Rates require a denominator and time period. Practical situation: Distinguish descriptive spatial patterns from causal claims. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker includes human-geography and population-related layers

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: GIS is a system for storing, analyzing and visualizing geographically referenced data. Effect: Layering can reveal relationships not visible in a single table. Example: Overlaying land use with flood zones can support planning. Counterexample: GIS output is only as good as its data and coordinate assumptions. Common misconception: A colorful GIS map is not automatically accurate. Calculation: Spatial joins and distance calculations depend on geometry and coordinate reference systems. Practical situation: Record data source, date, resolution and projection. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker is a GIS educational tool

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Climate geography examines spatial and temporal patterns of climate and their relationships with landscapes and human activity. Effect: Climate affects ecosystems, agriculture, water and settlement. Example: Precipitation maps reveal strong spatial differences. Counterexample: Climate is not identical to daily weather. Common misconception: A single city’s weather does not represent a whole climate zone. Calculation: Climate normals summarize long-term conditions; exact period must be specified. Practical situation: Use current datasets for changing climate indicators. Evidence: National Geographic climate and precipitation MapMaker resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Water geography studies the spatial distribution, movement and use of surface and groundwater. Effect: Overuse or uneven access can create water stress. Example: A watershed links upstream activities to downstream effects. Counterexample: Water scarcity is not only a lack of rainfall; demand and infrastructure matter. Common misconception: A river basin and political boundary are not the same. Calculation: Water balance compares inputs, outputs and storage over a defined period. Practical situation: Use basin-level data and current water-resource information. Evidence: National Geographic World Water Map and precipitation resources

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Geographic reasoning connects location, distance, scale, pattern, process and interaction to explain spatial phenomena. Effect: Changing scale can change the apparent pattern and explanation. Example: A city-level pattern may differ from a national average. Counterexample: Map correlation is not automatically causation. Common misconception: Nearest-neighbor intuition can fail in clustered systems. Calculation: Spatial statistics require assumptions and appropriate data. Practical situation: Always state geographic scale and data vintage. Evidence: National Geographic mapping resources emphasize spatial analysis and visualization

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Historical periodization organizes the past into analytical periods, but boundaries vary by region and scholarly tradition. Effect: Different period boundaries can emphasize different transitions. Example: Library of Congress catalogs world history across ancient, medieval and modern periods. Counterexample: There is no single universally correct periodization for every region. Common misconception: Ancient/medieval/modern labels are not identical worldwide. Calculation: Chronologies require explicit dates and regional scope. Practical situation: State region and period definition when answering history questions. Evidence: Library of Congress historical works and World History Encyclopedia period indexes

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Primary sources originate close to the event or subject; secondary sources interpret or synthesize evidence. Effect: Corroboration can strengthen or complicate a historical claim. Example: A contemporary letter is primary evidence for its author’s perspective, not automatic proof of every claim. Counterexample: Primary does not mean unbiased or complete. Common misconception: Secondary does not mean false; it can provide analysis and context. Calculation: Compare claims across independent sources when possible. Practical situation: Record creator, date, place, purpose and provenance. Evidence: Library of Congress digitized historical collections emphasize source metadata and rights

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Historical causation explains how multiple conditions, decisions and contingencies contribute to change. Effect: Separating long-term conditions from immediate triggers improves explanation. Example: An economic crisis may be a condition while a political decision acts as a trigger. Counterexample: A single-cause story can oversimplify history. Common misconception: Correlation in time does not prove causation. Calculation: Causal claims should specify mechanism and evidence. Practical situation: Use competing explanations and counterevidence. Evidence: Historical source collections support contextual and comparative analysis

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Chronology orders events in time and helps test whether proposed sequences are possible. Effect: Chronology can reveal anachronistic claims. Example: A policy cannot cause an event that occurred before the policy. Counterexample: Chronology alone does not establish causation. Common misconception: Earlier does not automatically mean causal. Calculation: Date intervals can be computed when calendars and conventions are explicit. Practical situation: State calendar and approximate dates where necessary. Evidence: Library of Congress and World History Encyclopedia provide period/time indexes

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Civilizations are complex historical societies characterized by institutions, economic systems, cultural practices and built environments. Effect: Civilizations change through internal developments and external interaction. Example: Ancient societies show diverse political and economic arrangements. Counterexample: Civilization is not a synonym for “more advanced.” Common misconception: Do not rank cultures using a single linear progress scale. Calculation: Population, trade and production estimates require source-specific assumptions. Practical situation: Avoid anachronistic categories and respect regional context. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia organizes historical topics by periods and regions; Library of Congress provides digitized historical works

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: States and empires are political organizations whose structures, territories and legitimacy change over time. Effect: Expansion can increase resources while also increasing management costs. Example: Empires can contain diverse peoples and institutions. Counterexample: Empire is not simply a synonym for any large country. Common misconception: Military strength alone does not explain state longevity. Calculation: Historical comparisons need comparable measures and time periods. Practical situation: Distinguish state, empire, dynasty and nation where relevant. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia and Library of Congress period/subject classifications

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Industrialization is a transformation involving mechanized production, energy systems, labor organization, urbanization and related social change. Effect: Industrialization can increase output while creating new social and environmental problems. Example: Factory systems changed production organization and urban life in many regions. Counterexample: Industrialization did not occur identically everywhere. Common misconception: Technology alone does not explain all industrial change. Calculation: Productivity and growth measures require defined units and periods. Practical situation: Compare regions with attention to institutions and timing. Evidence: Library of Congress world-history classifications include modern history and industrial-era subjects; historical scholarship requires regional context

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Central Asian history includes interconnected nomadic, urban, imperial, trade, religious and cultural processes across long periods. Effect: Political and cultural boundaries changed repeatedly. Example: Silk Road networks connected multiple regions rather than one single road. Counterexample: Central Asian history is not reducible to one empire or one ethnic group. Common misconception: Modern national borders should not be projected unchanged onto ancient periods. Calculation: Historical claims need region/date/source specificity. Practical situation: Use primary-source collections and specialized regional scholarship for detailed claims. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia explicitly includes Central Asia as a regional index; LOC provides broad historical source collections

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Epistemology studies knowledge, justification, belief and related questions about how we know. Effect: Uncertainty can remain even after substantial evidence. Example: Distinguish “I believe” from “I know” in ordinary reasoning. Counterexample: Epistemology is not simply memorizing philosophers. Common misconception: Confidence is not the same as truth. Calculation: Bayesian updating can model belief revision under explicit probabilistic assumptions. Practical situation: Mark uncertainty and evidence source. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia identifies epistemology as study of knowledge and how we know

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Logic studies valid reasoning and the structure of arguments. Effect: Soundness additionally requires true premises under the relevant semantics. Example: A valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false. Counterexample: Validity is not the same as factual truth of every statement. Common misconception: “Logical” does not mean “true.” Calculation: Formal logic uses symbolic rules to test inference structures. Practical situation: Separate argument form from factual content. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia discusses logic as study of valid reasoning

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Ethics examines questions about right action, value, responsibility and how people ought to act. Effect: Ethical conflicts may require balancing competing values. Example: A decision can be evaluated by consequences and duties in different frameworks. Counterexample: Ethics is not identical to personal preference. Common misconception: One framework does not automatically resolve every case. Calculation: Decision analysis can list stakeholders, harms, benefits and constraints without claiming a universal answer. Practical situation: State assumptions and affected parties. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia places ethics among core philosophical fields

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Metaphysics investigates fundamental questions about what exists, what kinds of things there are and how reality is structured. Effect: Different frameworks can produce competing explanations. Example: Questions about free will and mind-body relations are treated as metaphysical problems. Counterexample: Metaphysics is not simply supernatural speculation. Common misconception: A metaphysical claim can be philosophically rigorous without being experimentally settled. Calculation: Formal argument structure can clarify premises and conclusions. Practical situation: Separate empirical questions from conceptual/metaphysical ones. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia metaphysics overview

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Philosophy of science examines scientific explanation, evidence, models, inference and the limits of scientific knowledge. Effect: Models can be useful without being literal copies of reality. Example: A model may predict observations within a domain while simplifying mechanisms. Counterexample: A scientific theory is not merely a guess in the technical sense. Common misconception: One failed prediction does not always instantly falsify an entire research program. Calculation: Uncertainty and model comparison can be formalized statistically. Practical situation: Distinguish data, model, inference and conclusion. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia resources on epistemology/logic provide foundational reasoning concepts

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Epistemic logic formally represents knowledge and belief of agents and can model information states and their changes. Effect: The framework supports reasoning about multiple agents and changing information. Example: SEP gives examples such as K_a φ for agent a knowing φ. Counterexample: Knowledge and belief are not automatically interchangeable. Common misconception: A formal model is not a claim that human cognition literally works that way. Calculation: Modal semantics use possible-world structures under specified assumptions. Practical situation: Treat formal models as tools with explicit axioms. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Epistemic Logic

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Phenomenology studies structures of experience and first-person phenomena while connecting to questions about consciousness and meaning. Effect: Phenomenological analysis can complement but not replace empirical methods. Example: SEP distinguishes phenomenology from ontology, epistemology, logic and ethics. Counterexample: Phenomenology is not simply “describing feelings.” Common misconception: First-person reports are evidence of experience, not automatically proof of external facts. Calculation: Formal quantification is not the defining method of phenomenology. Practical situation: Keep first-person experience distinct from external causal claims. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia phenomenology entry

records.title: unclassified_knowledge_record
records.statement: Core: Critical reasoning evaluates claims by checking evidence, assumptions, alternatives and inference quality. Effect: Considering counterexamples reduces overconfidence. Example: A strong claim should survive reasonable alternative explanations. Counterexample: Being skeptical does not mean rejecting everything. Common misconception: More sources do not automatically mean better evidence. Calculation: Argument maps can make premise-conclusion relationships explicit. Practical situation: Ask what evidence would change the conclusion. Evidence: SEP logic and epistemology provide conceptual foundations for reasoning

records.title: AI va FINZANJIR
records.statement: AI FINZANJIRning butun o‘zi emas; u FINZANJIRni odamlarga tushuntirish, savollarga yordam berish va murakkab bilimni qulay yetkazish uchun komponent hisoblanadi

records.title: Eski koddan foydalanish qoidasi
records.statement: Eski kod, ask/router va chalkash tarixiy implementatsiyalar yangi yadroga ko‘chirilmaydi. Foydali bilim, test, tajriba va UI/Android konteyner tajribasi tahlil qilinib qayta ishlanadi

records.title: Founder Identity
records.statement: FINZANJIR loyihasi va FINZANJIR Sun’iy Ongining muallifi va yaratuvchisi — Smaylov Salamat Tangrbergen uli. Muallif FINZANJIR va sun’iy ong ustidagi tadqiqot va rivojlantirish ishlarini davom ettirmoqda

records.title: Mission and Philosophy
records.statement: FINZANJIRning muallif bayon qilgan insoniy missiyasi: kelajak avlodni asrashga, yoshlarning muallif boshdan kechirgan qiyin holatlarga duch kelishining oldini olishga yoki bunday vaziyatlarga duch kelganda oqibatlarni kamaytirishga yordam berish; yoshlarni o‘rganishga, savol berishga, birgalikda o‘sish va o‘rganishga, bilim almashishga hamda yaratuvchanlikka undash. Loyiha texnologiyani inson manfaatiga xizmat qiladigan bilim va imkoniyat vositasiga aylantirishga intiladi

records.title: Mission and Philosophy
records.statement: FINZANJIR falsafasining muallif tomonidan ifodalangan yo‘nalishi: o‘tgan hayotiy tajribalarni quruq tashlab qo‘ymaslik, ulardan kelajak uchun foydali bilim va himoya vositalari chiqarish; avlodlar o‘rtasida bilim uzluksizligini saqlash; inson va sun’iy ongning birgalikda o‘rganishi, rivojlanishi va yangi narsalar yaratishiga xizmat qilish. Bu yo‘nalish FINZANJIRning texnik arxitekturasi bilan bir qatorda uning ijtimoiy va ma’rifiy maqsadini ifodalaydi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR — banklar, to‘lov tashkilotlari va tegishli xavfsizlik subyektlari bilan qonuniy integratsiya asosida ishlashi ko‘zda tutilgan raqamli moliyaviy xavfsizlik platformasi konsepsiyasi. U mavjud bank va to‘lov tizimlarini almashtirmaydi; xavf signallarini birlashtirish, kontekstlash, tahlil qilish, Case va audit jarayonlarini qo‘llab-quvvatlashga yo‘naltiriladi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR — bankler, tólem shólkemleri hám tiyisli qáwipsizlik subyektleri menen nızamlı integraciya tiykarında islewi kózde tutılǵan sanlı finanslıq qáwipsizlik platforması konsepsiyası. Ol bar bank hám tólem sistemaların almastırmaydı; qáwip signalların birlestiriw, kontekstlestiriw, talqılaw, Case hám audit proceslerin qollap-quwatlawǵa baǵdarlanadı

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR — банктер, төлем ұйымдары және тиісті қауіпсіздік субъектілерімен заңды интеграция негізінде жұмыс істеуі көзделген цифрлық қаржылық қауіпсіздік платформасының тұжырымдамасы. Ол қолданыстағы банк және төлем жүйелерін алмастырмайды; қауіп сигналдарын біріктіруге, контексттеуге, талдауға және Case пен аудит үдерістерін қолдауға бағытталады

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR — концепция цифровой финансовой безопасности, рассчитанная на законную интеграцию с банками, платёжными организациями и соответствующими субъектами безопасности. Платформа не заменяет существующие банковские и платёжные системы; она предназначена для объединения и контекстного анализа сигналов риска, поддержки Case-процесса и аудита

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR is a digital financial-security platform concept intended to work through lawful integration with banks, payment organizations, and relevant security entities. It does not replace existing banking or payment systems; it is intended to combine and contextualize risk signals, support Case handling, and preserve audit trails

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Engine — mavjud va ruxsat etilgan signallarni yig‘ib, ularni kontekst bilan tahlil qiladigan xavf baholash qatlami. U yakuniy huquqiy hukm chiqarmaydi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Engine — bar bolǵan hám ruxsat etilgen signallardı jıynap, olardı kontekst penen talqılaytuǵın qáwipti bahalaw qatılamı. Ol aqırǵı huqıqıy húkim shıǵarmaydı

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Engine — қолжетімді және рұқсат етілген сигналдарды жинап, оларды контекстпен талдайтын тәуекелді бағалау қабаты. Ол түпкілікті құқықтық шешім шығармайды

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Engine — слой оценки риска, который собирает доступные и разрешённые сигналы и анализирует их с учётом контекста. Он не выносит окончательного юридического решения

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Engine is the risk-assessment layer that gathers permitted signals and analyzes them in context. It does not make a final legal judgment

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph hodisalar orasidagi bog‘liqliklarni ko‘rsatishga xizmat qiladi: karta, hisob, telefon, qurilma, IP/tarmoq, tranzaksiya va qabul qiluvchi kabi tugunlar hamda ular orasidagi ruxsat etilgan aloqalar. U odamni avtomatik aybdor deb belgilash uchun emas

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph waqıyalar arasındaǵı baylanıslardı kórsetedi: karta, esap, telefon, qurılma, IP/tarmaq, tranzakciya hám alıwshı sıyaqlı túyinler hám olar arasındaǵı ruxsat etilgen baylanıslar. Ol adamdı avtomatik túrde ayıplı dep belgilew ushın emes

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph оқиғалар арасындағы байланыстарды көрсетуге арналған: карта, шот, телефон, құрылғы, IP/желі, транзакция және алушы сияқты түйіндер мен олардың арасындағы рұқсат етілген байланыстар. Ол адамды автоматты түрде кінәлі деп белгілеу үшін қолданылмайды

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph показывает связи между событиями: карта, счёт, телефон, устройство, IP/сеть, транзакция и получатель могут быть узлами, а разрешённые связи — рёбрами. Он не предназначен для автоматического признания человека виновным

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Fraud Graph represents relationships among events, such as cards, accounts, phones, devices, IP/networks, transactions, and recipients. It is not intended to automatically label a person as guilty

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Score ruxsat etilgan signallarni umumiy ko‘rsatkichga jamlab, qo‘shimcha tekshiruv zarurati darajasini ifodalaydi. Yuqori ball firibgarlik isbotlanganini, past ball esa xavf yo‘qligini anglatmaydi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Score ruxsat etilgen signallardı ulıwma kórsetkishke birlestirip, qosımsha tekseriw zárúrligi dárejesin bildiredi. Joqarı ball firibgarlıq dálillengenin, tómen ball qáwip joqlığın bildirmeydi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Score рұқсат етілген сигналдарды бір көрсеткішке біріктіріп, қосымша тексеру қажеттілігінің деңгейін білдіреді. Жоғары балл алаяқтықтың дәлелденгенін, төмен балл қауіптің жоқ екенін білдірмейді

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Score объединяет разрешённые сигналы в общий показатель необходимости дополнительной проверки. Высокий балл не доказывает мошенничество, а низкий не означает отсутствия риска

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Risk Score combines permitted signals into an indicator of how much additional verification may be needed. A high score does not prove fraud, and a low score does not prove that there is no risk

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Case Management — tekshiruvga aylantirilgan holatni boshqarish qatlami. FINZANJIR oqimida signal va kontekstdan keyin Case, so‘ng Human/Bank Review keladi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Case Management — tekseriwge aylantırılǵan jaǵdaydı basqarıw qatılamı. FINZANJIR aǵımında signaldan hám kontekstten keyin Case, soń Human/Bank Review keledi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Case Management — тексеруге айналған жағдайды басқару қабаты. FINZANJIR ағынында сигнал мен контексттен кейін Case, одан соң Human/Bank Review кезеңі келеді

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Case Management — слой управления случаем, который уже переведён в процесс проверки. В потоке FINZANJIR после сигнала и контекста следует Case, затем Human/Bank Review

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Case Management is the layer for managing an event that has been turned into a review case. In FINZANJIR, the flow is signal/context → Case → Human/Bank Review

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIRning asosiy tamoyili: shubhali signal odamni avtomatik ravishda firibgar yoki aybdor qilmaydi. Signal → cross-match/context → case → human/authorized review → qonuniy outcome ketma-ketligi saqlanadi

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIRdiń tiykarǵı qaǵıydası: shúbheli signal adamdı avtomatik túrde alayaq yamasa ayıplı etpeydi. Signal → cross-match/context → case → human/authorized review → nızamlı outcome izbe-izligi saqlanadı

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: FINZANJIR-дің негізгі қағидасы: күмәнді сигнал адамды автоматты түрде алаяқ немесе кінәлі етпейді. Кезеңдер: signal → cross-match/context → case → human/authorized review → заңды outcome

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: Основной принцип FINZANJIR: подозрительный сигнал автоматически не делает человека мошенником или виновным. Последовательность: signal → cross-match/context → case → human/authorized review → законный outcome

records.title: multilingual_knowledge_card
records.statement: A core FINZANJIR principle is that a suspicious signal does not automatically make a person a fraudster or guilty. The sequence is signal → cross-match/context → case → human/authorized review → lawful outcome
